Largest country in South America (pop. over 214 million), with its capital at [[Brasília]]. Fifth-largest in the world by area (8,515,770 sq km) and seventh by population, Brazil is a federation of 26 states and a Federal District. Its most populous city is [[São Paulo]], followed by [[Rio de Janeiro]]. [[Portuguese language|Portuguese]] is the official language, and Brazil is the only Portuguese-speaking country in the Americas.

Bounded by the Atlantic Ocean on the east, with a coastline of 7,491 km, Brazil covers roughly half of the continent and borders every other South American country except Ecuador and Chile. It contains most of the Amazon basin, with the world's largest river system and most extensive virgin tropical forest, and ranks first among 17 megadiverse countries.

Indigenous peoples inhabited the territory before the Portuguese explorer [[Pedro Álvares Cabral]] landed in 1500. Portugal founded the first city, São Vicente, in 1532 and imported enslaved Africans to work plantations. Prince Pedro of Braganza declared independence in 1822 and established the [[Empire of Brazil]]. Slavery was finally abolished in 1888, and a military coup in 1889 made Brazil a presidential republic. A revolution in 1930 brought [[Getúlio Vargas]] to power. A military dictatorship ruled from 1964 until 1985, and the constitution of 1988 defines Brazil as a democratic federal republic.

Brazil has the largest economy in Latin America and one of the 10 largest in the world. It is a founding member of the United Nations and a member of the G20 and [[BRICS]].

Baked food made from water, flour, and often yeast. A staple food across the world, particularly in Europe and the Middle East, bread is one of the oldest human-made foods. The oldest evidence of bread-making comes from a 14,500-year-old Natufian site in Jordan's northeastern desert, and grains became its mainstay around 10,000 BC with the dawn of the [[Neolithic]] age and the spread of agriculture.

Bread may be leavened by naturally occurring microbes, as in [[Sourdough|sourdough]], by chemicals, by industrially produced [[Yeast|yeast]], or by high-pressure aeration; it may also be unleavened. In yeast fermentation, carbon dioxide and ethanol vapors produce the air pockets of the crumb. An early leavened bread was baked as early as 6000 BC in southern Mesopotamia, home of the [[Sumer|Sumerian]] civilization, which may have passed the knowledge to the Egyptians around 3000 BC. [[Pliny the Elder]] reported that the Gauls and Iberians used the foam skimmed from beer, called barm, for a lighter bread, and that the most common leavening was a piece of dough kept from the previous day. The Chorleywood process, developed in 1961, uses intense mechanical working to shorten fermentation and is widely used in large factories.

Bread is the staple of the Middle East, Central Asia, North Africa, Europe, and European-derived cultures, in contrast to parts of South and East Asia, where rice or noodles are the staple. Most is made from [[Wheat|wheat]], whose gluten gives dough sponginess and elasticity. Other cereals, including [[Rye|rye]], barley, maize, oats, sorghum, millet, and rice, have been used, usually mixed with wheat flour because they contain less gluten. Gluten-free breads use flours such as almond, rice, sorghum, corn, legumes, and cassava.

Structure designed to span an obstacle, such as a river or railway, and carry vehicles, pedestrians, and other loads across it. Most bridges consist of a flat deck supported by beams, arches, or cables, resting on a [[Foundation (engineering)|foundation]] designed to transfer the bridge's weight to the subsoil without settling.

The earliest bridges were wooden boardwalks or logs across wetlands and creeks. Corbel arch bridges were built c. 13th century BC in Mycenaean Greece, and the Arkadiko Bridge still exists. The Romans and ancient Chinese built major arch bridges of timber, stone, and brick; the Romans also used cement, mixed with small rocks to form [[Concrete|concrete]]. Trajan's Bridge (c. 105 AD) crossed the [[Danube]] and was over 900 m long. The Anji Bridge, built from 595 to 605 AD during the [[Sui dynasty]], is the oldest surviving stone bridge in China. The Inca built rope suspension bridges in the [[Andes]]. In Renaissance Europe, scientific and engineering advances produced wider spans, truss bridges, and stone segmental arches.

The [[Industrial Revolution]] brought mass-produced [[Steel|steel]], which enabled truss and cantilever bridges able to cross wide rivers and deep valleys. The longest spans use suspension or cable-stayed designs, both relying on high-strength steel cables, and the maximum span reached 2 km in 2022. Other forms include viaducts, trestles, and movable bridges such as drawbridges and swing bridges.

A bridge must support its own weight and that of its traffic, and tolerate stresses from winds, floods, and earthquakes; engineers typically use limit state design and the finite element method. Bridges can shorten transport times and raise gross domestic product, but can also increase pollution. Some serve as landmarks, such as the [[Golden Gate Bridge]].

Dominions, colonies, protectorates, mandates, and other territories ruled or administered by the United Kingdom and its predecessor states. By 1913 it held sway over 412 million people, 23 percent of the world population, and by 1920 it covered 35.5 million sq km, 24 percent of the Earth's land area.

Britain became a major power in the Indian subcontinent after the [[East India Company]] conquered Mughal Bengal at the Battle of Plassey in 1757. The [[American Revolution]] cost it some of its oldest and most populous colonies by 1783, and expansion turned toward Asia, Africa, and the Pacific. After the defeat of France in the [[Napoleonic Wars]] (1803–15), Britain was the principal naval and imperial power of the 19th century. It abolished the slave trade in 1807 and slavery itself across its territories in 1833.

The empire's growth involved military campaigns, resource extraction, and policies that exacerbated famines and provoked local resistance, and historians debate the balance between exploitation and modernization in colonial rule.

The empire reached its largest extent after [[World War I]]. In [[World War II]], its colonies in East and Southeast Asia were occupied by Japan. India, its most valuable and populous possession, became independent in 1947, and most other territories followed. The [[Suez Crisis]] of 1956 confirmed Britain's decline as a global power, and the handover of Hong Kong to China on July 1, 1997, symbolized for many its end. Fourteen overseas territories remain British, and many former colonies joined the [[Commonwealth of Nations]].

Distribution of audio and audiovisual content to dispersed audiences through an electronic mass communications medium, typically by [[Radio wave|radio waves]] in a one-to-many model. Broadcasting began with AM radio, which became popular around 1920 with the spread of [[Vacuum tube|vacuum tube]] transmitters and receivers.

The term comes from the agricultural method of sowing seeds by casting them broadly. Applications to one-to-many radio transmissions appeared as early as 1898. Over-the-air, or terrestrial, broadcasting is usually associated with radio and television and in most countries requires a license. Transmission by wire, as in [[Cable television|cable television]], also counts, and since the 2000s streaming has increasingly been called broadcasting as well. U.S. federal regulations define broadcasting as transmissions intended for reception by the general public, so amateur and citizens band radio operators may not broadcast.

In 1894 Italian inventor [[Guglielmo Marconi]] began developing wireless communication using radio waves, and by 1901 had shown they could cross the Atlantic. In 1904 a commercial service began sending nightly news summaries to ships. [[World War I]] accelerated military radio, and commercial AM broadcasting began in the 1920s. Stereo FM broadcasting began in the 1930s in the United States and the 1970s in the United Kingdom.

[[John Logie Baird]] demonstrated moving pictures at Selfridges in London on March 25, 1925, and the British Broadcasting Corporation began experimental broadcasts on September 30, 1929. Most 20th-century televisions used the cathode-ray tube; a promising version was produced by [[Philo Farnsworth]] and demonstrated on September 7, 1927. Satellite broadcasting began in the 1960s, and in the 2000s broadcasters switched from analog to digital signals.

Period in the development of material culture among ancient societies in Asia, the Near East, and Europe, marked by the use of [[Bronze|bronze]]. It is the middle period of the three-age system, following the [[Stone Age]] and preceding the [[Iron Age]]; a transition, the [[Chalcolithic]], separates it from the [[Neolithic]]. The Bronze Age had begun in much of the Old World by 3,000 BC. In the Near East it ran c. 3300–1200 BC, in Europe from about 2500 BC to 800 BC, and in East Asia it began around 2000 BC.

Bronze Age cultures were the first to develop writing: cuneiform in Mesopotamia and hieroglyphs in Egypt. The Americas are conventionally studied under a five-period system with no Bronze Age.

Bronze was harder and more durable than other metals then available. Iron is abundant, but smelting it requires 1,250 °C, and it was beyond common use until the end of the 2nd millennium BC. Tin occurs in few places, unlike copper, so bronze often stayed rare and expensive, and some societies used it mainly for weapons or elite art. The Maykop culture of the North Caucasus produced the oldest-known bronze, an arsenical bronze, by the mid-4th millennium BC.

The Near East entered the Bronze Age first, with the rise of [[Sumer]] in the mid-4th millennium BC. Its cultures developed city-states, written law codes, and the potter's wheel. The Hittites founded an empire in the 18th century BC at Hattusa, reaching its height in the 14th century BC. Widespread disruption in the eastern Mediterranean around 1200 BC, the [[Late Bronze Age collapse]], ended the age there.

[[Alloy]] consisting primarily of [[Copper|copper]], commonly with about 12–12.5% [[Tin|tin]]. Added metals such as aluminum, manganese, nickel, or zinc, and sometimes phosphorus, arsenic, or silicon, give alloys harder than copper alone or with other useful properties.

The period in which bronze was the hardest metal in widespread use is the [[Bronze Age]]. It began in western Eurasia in the mid-4th millennium BC and in China in the early 2nd millennium BC, and was followed by the [[Iron Age]], which started about 1300 BC. The earliest known tin-copper artifact, dated to c. 4650 BC, comes from the Vinča culture site at Pločnik, Serbia. Copper–[[Arsenic|arsenic]] alloys, stronger and with a lower melting point than pure copper, were made earlier; the earliest known artifacts, from Tal-i-Iblis on the Iranian plateau, date to 3800–3400 BC. Tin became the major non-copper ingredient in the late 3rd millennium BC; tin bronze was easier to control and cast and, unlike arsenic, not toxic.

Copper and tin ores are seldom found together, with exceptions such as [[Cornwall]], so bronze work has always involved long-distance trade. Cornish tin was traded as far as Phoenicia. An analysis of 324 metallic finds of the Indus Valley Civilisation (2600–1900 BC) found 67 (20%) with some tin content.

Bronze has a Vickers hardness of 60–258, against 30–80 for wrought iron, yet the Bronze Age gave way to iron after migrations around 1200–1100 BC disrupted tin supplies and raised prices. Bronze remains in use for sculpture, bells, bearings, and marine hardware.

Indian religion and philosophy based on teachings attributed to [[The Buddha|the Buddha]], a wandering ascetic and religious teacher of the 6th or 5th century BC. The world's fourth-largest religion, it has an estimated 320 million to 540 million followers, about 4.1%–6.7% of the world population. It originated in the eastern Gangetic plain as a śramaṇa movement, spread through much of Asia via the [[Silk Road]], and reached the West in the 19th century.

According to tradition, the Buddha taught a path leading to awakening and liberation from dukkha (suffering, or unsatisfactoriness) by attaining [[Nirvana|nirvana]], the extinguishing of the passions. He described this path as a Middle Way between extreme asceticism and sensory indulgence. Widely observed teachings include the [[Four Noble Truths]], the Noble Eightfold Path, dependent origination, [[Karma|karma]], and the three marks of existence. Accounts of his life are inconsistent; tradition holds that he was born in Lumbini, achieved enlightenment at Bodh Gaya at age 35, taught for 45 years, and died about age 80 at Kushinagar.

The canon is vast, with textual collections in Sanskrit, Pali, Tibetan, and Chinese. Scholars generally recognize two major extant branches. [[Theravada]] (School of the Elders) emphasizes attaining nirvana to end the cycle of death and rebirth and is followed mainly in Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, and Sri Lanka. [[Mahayana]] (Great Vehicle) emphasizes the bodhisattva ideal of working for the liberation of all sentient beings; it is the largest branch, predominant in East Asia, and includes Chan, Zen, Pure Land, and Nichiren. [[Vajrayana]], which incorporates esoteric tantric techniques, is practiced in Tibet and Mongolia and may be viewed as a separate branch or as part of Mahayana.

Enclosed structure with a roof and walls, usually standing permanently in one place, such as a house or factory. Buildings vary in size, shape, and function and have adapted over history to available materials, weather, land prices, ground conditions, specific uses, prestige, and aesthetics. They serve needs including shelter from weather, security, living space, privacy, and storage. The word structure is used more broadly, including formations without walls, such as fences. Interest in sustainable planning has made green buildings an intentional part of the design of many new ones.

There is clear evidence of homebuilding from around 18,000 BC, and buildings became common during the Neolithic period. Common materials include brick, concrete, stone, and combinations of them. In the 19th and 20th centuries steel framing and reinforced concrete allowed unprecedented heights, as in the [[Skyscraper|skyscraper]]. The distinction between low-rise and high-rise is debated, but generally three stories or less is low-rise.

Residential buildings include single-family [[House|houses]], duplexes, and [[Apartment|apartment]] buildings, as well as institutions such as nursing homes, orphanages, and prisons. Yurts and motorhomes are considered dwellings but not buildings. Commercial buildings house at least one business and no residents, such as stores, restaurants, and [[Hotel|hotels]]. Industrial buildings, such as [[Factory|factories]] and [[Warehouse|warehouses]], are those in which heavy industry takes place. Agricultural buildings are outbuildings on farms, such as [[Barn|barns]]. Some buildings mix uses, commonly commercial and residential, and a group of interrelated buildings may be called a complex.

Designing, constructing, and operating a building is a collective effort of developers, financiers, local planning authorities, construction managers, and licensed [[Architecture|architects]] and engineers.

Organization or activity engaged in producing or buying and selling goods and services, usually for [[Profit (economics)|profit]]. Individuals who work neither for a government agency nor for a mission-driven nonprofit are almost always employed in the private sector, by businesses whose primary goal is to generate profit through the creation and capture of economic value above cost.

Forms of ownership vary by jurisdiction. A sole proprietorship is owned by one person, who has unlimited liability for the business's obligations and is personally taxed on all its income. A [[Partnership|partnership]] is owned by two or more people; in most forms each partner has unlimited liability for its debts. A [[Corporation|corporation]] is a legal entity separate from its shareholders, who have limited liability. Privately owned corporations may be held by a small group or publicly held, with shares traded on a [[Stock exchange|stock exchange]]. A cooperative has members rather than shareholders, who share decision-making authority. In a franchise, entrepreneurs purchase the right to open and run a business from a larger corporation; in the United States, one out of twelve retail businesses is franchised, employing 8 million people.

The management theorist Peter Drucker defined the purpose of a business as creating a customer, with profit an essential condition for survival rather than the primary goal. Marketing scholar Philip Kotler has similarly said a business exists primarily to serve. Businesses have driven technological advance and raised living standards since the Industrial Revolution, though critics point to monopolistic behavior and environmental impacts, which prompt regulation.
